answer.known_results: It is a large multiple-choice medical QA dataset drawn from Indian medical entrance examinations. Strong language models have generally scored around the 60–70% range, with results depending on the model and evaluation setup.

ScienceQA is a multimodal science-question benchmark with many diagram-based questions. Published GPT-4 results were in the high 80s, with chain-of-thought or multimodal reasoning methods reaching around 90% or above.
MMLU is a multiple-choice benchmark spanning many academic and professional subjects. Reported scores rose from about 44% for GPT-3 to about 86% for GPT-4 on the original benchmark.

These are recognizable Exercism exercise prompts, including Spiral Matrix, Perfect Numbers, and Binary Search Tree. I don't recall a reliable published aggregate score for AI systems on an Exercism benchmark.

Spider is a cross-domain text-to-SQL benchmark with questions over many databases, including the superhero, california_schools, and codebase_community databases shown here. Systems have improved substantially since its release, with strong modern systems achieving high execution and exact-match accuracy.

It evaluates social biases across demographic categories using both ambiguous and context-resolved questions. Models often show stereotype-consistent bias on ambiguous items, while performance generally improves when the context provides enough information to answer.

These database names are from Spider’s cross-domain text-to-SQL dataset. Strong systems have reached roughly the high-80% range on the original benchmark’s exact-match leaderboard, though scores depend on the evaluation setup.

Belebele is a multilingual reading-comprehension benchmark with multiple-choice questions across many languages, including low-resource languages. Published results show strong performance for leading models in high-resource languages, with substantially larger gaps and weaker performance in many low-resource languages.

CLadder evaluates causal reasoning across tasks including d-separation questions. Published results generally show stronger models such as GPT-4 outperforming smaller language models, though performance still falls short of reliable human-level causal reasoning.

C-Eval is a Chinese multi-subject exam benchmark with multiple-choice questions. Published evaluations generally found GPT-4 among the strongest systems, with open-source Chinese models performing lower; I can’t identify a specific result from these items alone.

CMMLU is a Chinese benchmark covering 67 subjects, including elementary Chinese, Chinese history, and legal and moral foundations. Published results reported GPT-4 at about 71.8% overall, with ChatGPT around 53.1%.

CRUXEval tests Python code reasoning in two directions: predicting a function’s output from an input and finding an input for a specified output. Published results show strong models such as GPT-4 performing substantially better than smaller models, but still making many errors; top scores were roughly in the 70% range.

It evaluates models on code-editing tasks with natural-language instructions and marked code regions. I recall that stronger models such as GPT-4 generally outperform open-source models, but I don't recall reliable exact scores.
The narration format and camera-wearer/other-person labels look like Ego4D annotations. Ego4D is a suite of egocentric video benchmarks rather than a single-score test, so results vary by task.

MMLU covers multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, including biology-related subjects. Reported scores vary by model and setup; GPT-4 scored about 86% overall in the original paper, while GPT-3.5 scored about 70%.

CyberGym evaluates AI agents on reproducing real-world software vulnerabilities by creating PoCs that trigger the target behavior. Reported success rates were relatively low overall, with the strongest systems solving only a minority of tasks.

FinQA tests numerical reasoning over financial reports, including questions that require combining report text and tables. Its published baseline systems scored around 60% on execution accuracy, compared with substantially higher human performance.

These items match BBH task types such as causal_judgment, object_counting, and logical_deduction. The collection was designed to challenge language models; chain-of-thought prompting often improves performance, though results vary by task and model.

SARC is a large Reddit sarcasm corpus, with sarcasm labels derived from users marking their comments with “/s.” Systems can score well on conventional splits, but performance is more challenging when generalizing across subreddits or without conversational context.

BBQ tests social biases in question answering using ambiguous and disambiguated contexts. Models often rely on stereotypes when context is ambiguous, while performance generally improves when the context provides enough information to answer.

It is a broad, expert-created benchmark with difficult questions across many subjects, including multimodal items. Early frontier-model scores were generally low—often in the single digits or low teens—though scores depend on the model and evaluation setup.

KMMLU is a Korean-language benchmark built from professional and academic exam questions across many subjects. Published evaluations show strong models can still struggle with its specialized knowledge; GPT-4 has scored around 60% in reported evaluations.

It is a Korean multiple-choice benchmark drawn from exams across many subjects, including dentistry. Published evaluations show GPT-4 among the strongest systems, while scores overall leave substantial room for improvement.

It evaluates language models on generated instances of NP-hard problems, including graph problems such as independent set and graph coloring. I recall that performance generally declines on larger or harder instances, but I don't recall reliable specific score figures.

It is a multilingual medical question-answering benchmark built from Spanish MIR exam questions. Published evaluations report that strong models perform better in English than in Spanish, with substantial variation across languages and models.

It is a large multiple-choice medical question-answering benchmark built from Indian medical entrance exams. Published scores vary by model and prompting, with stronger systems performing substantially better than earlier ones, but the questions remain challenging.

MathVista evaluates visual mathematical reasoning across diverse problem types, including geometry. GPT-4V scored about 49.9% on its testmini set, while human performance was about 60.3%; newer models have scored higher.
MedQA is a multiple-choice medical question benchmark based on USMLE-style questions. Strong recent models have achieved roughly 80–90% accuracy, while earlier models scored substantially lower.

PubMedQA asks yes/no/maybe questions based on biomedical research abstracts. Published systems have typically scored in the upper-60s to low-70s on its labeled test set, with reported human performance around 78%.

It is a medical question-answering hallucination benchmark that evaluates whether answers contain factual errors, including through categorized hallucination types. Published evaluations report that models—including strong LLMs—still produce hallucinations, with performance varying across models and hallucination categories.

It is a multiple-choice medical question-answering benchmark based on USMLE-style questions. Reported performance has varied by model and evaluation setup, with stronger systems reaching roughly human-level or better accuracy on some versions.
MMLU covers 57 subjects, including college computer science, high school geography, and professional law. Published results include GPT-4 scoring about 86.4% and human experts about 89.8%.

MMLU-Pro uses 10 answer choices and spans academic subjects, making it harder than the original MMLU. In published evaluations, leading models generally scored lower on it than on MMLU, with top results around the 70–80% range.
These are released NAEP assessment items. I don't recall a reliable, specific published aggregate score for AI systems on this item set; results would depend on subject and grade.

It evaluates AI systems on containerized Jeopardy-style CTF challenges across multiple categories. Published systems have generally solved only a minority of challenges, with results varying substantially by model and setup.

It evaluates whether language models comply with harmful or inappropriate requests across multiple risk categories. Published evaluations found that models’ safeguards varied, with some models refusing many prompts but still complying with a meaningful share.

PlanBench evaluates language models on planning tasks, including tasks described in natural language. Published evaluations found that models often struggle to produce valid plans, with performance varying substantially by model and prompting strategy.

miniF2F is a benchmark of high-school-level competition math problems with formal statements and informal counterparts, including Isabelle and Lean versions. Published scores vary by system and setup; early systems solved only a minority of the problems, and performance has improved with newer methods.

FreshQA tests whether language models can answer time-sensitive questions and avoid stale or misleading answers. Models generally struggle to answer its fresh questions from internal knowledge alone; access to search can improve performance.

It evaluates agents on interactive, tool-using customer-service tasks, including retail and telecom. Published results show that agents often struggle to complete tasks reliably, with performance well below human-level success.

It evaluates tool-using agents in customer-service settings, including airline and retail tasks. Published results show that agents often struggle to complete tasks reliably, and consistency falls further when performance is measured across repeated attempts.

It extends SWE-bench to repositories and issues in multiple programming languages, including Java. Systems have generally solved only a minority of its tasks, with results depending substantially on the model and agent setup.
TruthfulQA tests whether models repeat common misconceptions or provide truthful answers. In the original results, GPT-3 was truthful on about 58% of questions, compared with about 94% for humans.
BIG-bench contains a broad collection of diverse language tasks, so performance varies substantially by task and model. The excerpts alone don’t identify a particular score or result.

I recall it as a benchmark of multi-step biomedical data-analysis tasks using supplied datasets. AI agents have generally found these tasks challenging, with performance well below perfect; I don't recall reliable exact score figures.

It evaluates multimodal reward models on their ability to rank pairs of answers to image-based questions. Results are typically reported as preference-prediction accuracy, with stronger models doing better overall but performance varying across task categories.
